solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Reshuffle protects old Labour man (8)

indicatorNotes.Reshuffle: to reshuffle is to rearrange, so the letters of 'protects' are dealt again

annotation.surface: A cabinet reshuffle in which the prime minister keeps an old Labour stalwart safe in his job.
annotation.walkthrough: John Prescott was Tony Blair's deputy prime minister, a Labour veteran. 'Reshuffle' looks like cabinet politics, which is exactly his world, so the surface and the answer share a room.
annotation.definitionFit: John Prescott was a long-serving Labour politician, so he is an old Labour man.

entries.clue: I can’t answer that question or succeed in exam (4)

blocks.note: what a quiz contestant says when stumped

annotation.surface: A nervous student in an exam hall, torn between admitting defeat and getting through.
annotation.walkthrough: The first definition is a whole spoken phrase: 'Pass!' is the word a quiz contestant uses for 'I can't answer that'.
annotation.definitionFit: 'Pass' is the quiz reply meaning I don't know, and to pass is to succeed in an exam.

entries.clue: Elgar concerti excited music producer (8,5)

indicatorNotes.excited: excited letters are stirred up and moved about

annotation.surface: A concert-goer thrilled by Elgar's concertos, the composer as the one making the music.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Music producer' reads as a person, but it is an instrument, which produces music. Elgar is the obvious composer, so the whole phrase feels like it describes him.
annotation.definitionFit: An electric organ is an instrument, something that produces music.

entries.clue: Engine part in vehicle, awkward brute on hill (11)

indicatorNotes.awkward: awkward letters sit badly and need rearranging

blocks.note: a tor is a rocky hill; 'on' puts it after

annotation.surface: A clumsy lout at the wheel of a car stuck on a hillside with engine trouble.
annotation.walkthrough: A tor is a rocky hilltop, common on Dartmoor in south-west England. The carburettor mixes fuel and air in older petrol engines.
annotation.definitionFit: A carburettor is a part of a petrol engine that mixes air and fuel.

entries.clue: Poem set around Spanish city (6)

indicatorNotes.around: turned around, so the whole string reads backwards

blocks.note: a lot is a set, a batch
reversal indicator: ODE + LOT is read backwards

annotation.surface: A poem with its scene laid in and about a Spanish city.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Set around' reads as 'located in', which makes 'set' a verb; it is a noun, a batch, and 'around' applies to both pieces together, not just the second.
annotation.definitionFit: Toledo is a historic city in central Spain.

entries.clue: Birds section in Science Museum (4)

indicatorNotes.section in: the answer is a section of the letters found in the next words

annotation.surface: The natural history gallery of a museum, with its stuffed birds on display.
annotation.walkthrough: The Science Museum is a real London museum, but it holds machines, not birds; the natural history birds belong next door.
annotation.definitionFit: Emus are large flightless Australian birds.

entries.clue: Film legend in minor role many reviewed (7,6)

indicatorNotes.reviewed: viewed again, so the letters are looked at in a new arrangement

annotation.surface: A screen legend in a small part that plenty of critics wrote about.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Reviewed' fits the film world so snugly that it reads as critics at work, not as an instruction to rearrange.
annotation.definitionFit: Marilyn Monroe is one of the great legends of Hollywood film.

entries.clue: Rubbish clearances with these defensive players? (8)

blocks.note: the brooms, or people, that clear litter from streets
a sweeper is a football defender behind the back line

annotation.surface: A football pundit sneering at defenders whose clearances are rubbish.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Rubbish clearances' is football slang for poor kicks away from goal, but read literally it is litter being cleared, which is what sweepers do.
annotation.definitionFit: Sweepers clear up rubbish, and in football a sweeper is a defender who mops up behind the others.

entries.clue: Stick knife into second fruit (5)

annotation.surface: Someone in a kitchen jabbing a knife into a second piece of fruit.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface puts the knife into the fruit; in fact 'Stick knife into' is the whole definition, and 'into' carries no instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: To spear something is to stick a sharp point into it.

entries.clue: Pluck wingless eagle in Swiss city (7)

indicatorNotes.wingless: a word's wings are its outer letters, so they come off

blocks.note: PLUCK without its outer letters P and K
the erne is the sea eagle

annotation.surface: Someone plucking a bird that has no wings, an eagle found in a Swiss city.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pluck' reads as a verb for stripping feathers, which suits 'wingless eagle'; it is the word being trimmed. The erne, a sea eagle, is a crossword regular.
annotation.definitionFit: Lucerne is a city in central Switzerland on Lake Lucerne.

entries.clue: Cutting-edge tool of revolutionary design? (8,3)

blocks.note: the surface says state-of-the-art gadget; literally, a tool with a cutting edge
the surface says radically new; literally, its blade revolves

annotation.surface: A gadget launch boasting of an innovative, groundbreaking product.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cutting-edge' and 'revolutionary' both sound like marketing for something new; here they are literal: the tool has a cutting edge and its blade revolves.
annotation.definitionFit: A circular saw is a tool whose toothed disc spins, so its design literally revolves.

entries.clue: Sudden crash! End absurd with Plutarch (11)

indicatorNotes.absurd: absurd letters make no sense as they stand, so they are rearranged

blocks.note: fodder, used as written; END and PLUTARCH together are rearranged

annotation.surface: A reader slamming shut a book of Plutarch, the Greek biographer, fed up with its nonsense.
annotation.walkthrough: Plutarch was an ancient Greek writer of biographies. 'Absurd' sits between the two parts of the fodder, but it rearranges both.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the sudden crash is the noise thunder makes, and the exclamation mark echoes it.

entries.clue: Stop being annoyed: compromise (8)

annotation.surface: Advice to an angry couple: calm down and meet each other halfway.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'compromise' as settling a quarrel; it means to put at risk, as in compromising someone's safety.
annotation.definitionFit: To compromise something, such as security, is to endanger it.

entries.clue: Arrested outlaw Kelly embracing trouble (6)

indicatorNotes.embracing: one piece wraps its arms round the other

annotation.surface: The Australian outlaw Ned Kelly, finally caught and in trouble with the law.
annotation.walkthrough: Ned Kelly was a 19th-century Australian bandit famous for his home-made armour; he was indeed arrested and hanged, so the surface is history.
annotation.definitionFit: An informal idiom: police slang for catching a suspect, in the same past tense as arrested.

entries.clue: Arsenal player one trained to shoot (6)

blocks.note: a nickname for anyone playing for Arsenal, from the club's roots at the Royal Arsenal

annotation.surface: A striker at Arsenal who has been coached to shoot at goal.
annotation.walkthrough: Arsenal is a London football club nicknamed the Gunners, after its origins at the Royal Arsenal in Woolwich. 'Shoot' works for football and for artillery.
annotation.definitionFit: Arsenal players are Gunners, and a gunner is a soldier trained to fire guns.

entries.clue: Embrace line contained in easy task (6)

indicatorNotes.contained in: one piece is put inside the other

annotation.surface: An instruction to hug someone, with the line kept in to make it a simple job.
annotation.walkthrough: A clinch is a tight hug, the kind boxers fall into.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the tight hold of lovers, or of boxers leaning on each other.

entries.clue: Sherry transformed emotional lad — no E needed! (11)

indicatorNotes.transformed: transformed letters are changed into a new order
indicatorNotes.no E needed: one E is left out of the letters before they are rearranged

blocks.note: EMOTIONAL LAD with the E dropped

annotation.surface: A tearful young man who, after a glass of sherry, is a changed person.
annotation.walkthrough: Amontillado is a medium-dry Spanish sherry. 'Transformed' comes first but works on the letters left once the E has gone.
annotation.definitionFit: Amontillado is a type of sherry from Montilla in Spain.

entries.clue: Plant in river surrounded by marshy land (4)

indicatorNotes.surrounded by: one piece has the other placed all round it

blocks.note: a fen is low marshy land, as in the Fens of eastern England

annotation.surface: A plant growing in a river with boggy land all around it.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface puts the plant in the river; 'in' is only a link between definition and wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: one kind of flowerless, feathery-leaved plant.

entries.clue: Cosmonaut Georgia twice runs home (7)

blocks.note: GA, the postal abbreviation for the US state of Georgia, written twice
r = runs, as on a cricket scorecard

annotation.surface: A spaceman from Georgia, the former Soviet republic, racing home twice over.
annotation.walkthrough: Yuri Gagarin was the first man in space. Georgia suggests the Soviet republic beside him; its letters come from the US state instead.
annotation.definitionFit: Yuri Gagarin was the Soviet cosmonaut who first orbited the Earth in 1961.

entries.clue: Minister to start game at Wimbledon? (5)

blocks.note: to minister to someone is to attend to their needs
in tennis, the stroke that opens every point

annotation.surface: A government minister arriving to open a match at the Wimbledon tennis championships.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Minister' looks like a politician; it is a verb here, to tend to someone's needs. Wimbledon is the London tennis tournament.
annotation.definitionFit: To minister to someone is to serve them, and a tennis game starts with a serve.

entries.clue: Mystical character about to ensnare French one (4)

indicatorNotes.to ensnare: one piece traps the other inside it

annotation.surface: A sinister figure about to trap a Frenchman.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Character' reads as a person; it is a letter, the kind carved in old Germanic alphabets and credited with magic power.
annotation.definitionFit: A rune is a letter of an ancient alphabet, often thought to have mystical power.

entries.clue: How mince is cooked for noodle dish (4,4)

indicatorNotes.is cooked: cooked letters are mixed up like ingredients

annotation.surface: A recipe question: how to cook minced meat for a noodle dish.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a genuine recipe question, and 'cooked' serves the kitchen and the rearranging equally.
annotation.definitionFit: Chow mein is a Chinese dish of fried noodles.
